messages.content: i'm stuck on problem set 2. what's the vanishing gradient problem?

Backpropagation multiplies one activation derivative per layer. For the sigmoid that derivative is at most **0.25**, so through ten layers the gradient can shrink by a factor of about a million.

The consequence is that the earliest layers receive almost no signal and effectively stop learning, while the later layers train normally. It is not that they learn slowly — they largely do not learn at all.
ok so why does relu fix it

Because its derivative is exactly 1 wherever the unit is active:

$$\text{ReLU}'(z) = \begin{cases} 1 & z > 0 \\ 0 & z \leq 0 \end{cases}$$

Multiplying by 1 does not shrink anything, so the gradient passes back through an active ReLU unchanged.

It does introduce a different problem. A unit that consistently receives negative input outputs zero and has zero gradient, so it can never recover — the *dying ReLU* problem. Leaky ReLU exists to give those units a small non-zero gradient.
can you show me the code for the backward pass

For the two-layer network from lecture:

```python
def backward(x, y, w1, b1, w2, b2, cache):
    z1, a1, z2, y_hat = cache
    n = len(x)

    # Output layer
    delta2 = (y_hat - y) / n
    grad_w2 = delta2.T @ a1
    grad_b2 = delta2.sum(axis=0)

    # Hidden layer — note the elementwise product with the activation derivative.
    # This is the term that shrinks the gradient as depth increases.
    delta1 = (delta2 @ w2) * sigmoid_prime(z1)
    grad_w1 = delta1.T @ x
    grad_b1 = delta1.sum(axis=0)

    return grad_w1, grad_b1, grad_w2, grad_b2
```

The line to look at is `delta1`. Every layer you add inserts another `* sigmoid_prime(...)` into that chain, and each one is at most 0.25.
what's the difference between all the regularization things again, i keep mixing up l1 and l2

The short version: **L2 shrinks weights toward zero, L1 sets them to zero.**

| | Penalty | Effect | Use when |
|---|---|---|---|
| L2 (ridge) | $\lambda \sum w_j^2$ | Weights become small | Default for most models |
| L1 (lasso) | $\lambda \sum \lvert w_j \rvert$ | Some weights become exactly 0 | You want feature selection |

The geometric reason is worth knowing: L2's constraint region is a circle, so the loss contour touches it off-axis and both weights stay non-zero. L1's is a diamond with corners on the axes, and the contour tends to touch a corner — which sits exactly on an axis, meaning one weight is precisely zero.

fine. one more — is this right? if the training loss keeps going down but validation loss goes up then i should just train for longer because eventually it'll come back down right

No — that is the one situation where training longer actively makes things worse.

What you are describing is **overfitting**. The model is fitting structure that is specific to the training sample, and validation loss rising is the signal that it has started doing so. It will not come back down; the gap will keep widening.

The standard response is *early stopping*: keep the weights from the epoch where validation loss was at its minimum, and stop. It is the cheapest regulariser available, because you already have the validation set.
